name: arm7-multirate
title: Arm 7 — Multi-rate scheduler stress test (process-bigraph
question: When a composite is genuinely multi-rate (many independent instances each on a different coupling interval — the mismatched-interval case arms 1-6 avoid), does process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler reduce the per-tick O(P) due-scan to O(log P), so the many-rate run scales as ~O(P log P) instead of O(P^2) — and does it stay bit-identical to the stock scan loop?
hypothesis: Selecting the #270 event-heap scheduler (scheduler="heap") on a composite of N independent monolithic glycolysis instances with geometrically-spaced intervals runs the SAME math as the stock scan loop (bit-identical results) while popping only the due processes per tick and dropping horizon- overrunning ones, so its wall-clock advantage over scan grows monotonically with the instance count P.
objective: Build a genuinely multi-rate composite (the case the decision table otherwise says to avoid) and measure the stock-scan vs #270-heap wall-clock as P grows, confirming the scheduler — not the biology — is what changes, and that scan and heap agree to the bit.
description: Methods arm of the SBML-decomposition investigation. Unlike arms 1-6 (equal coupling intervals, the cheap regime), arm 7 deliberately builds N INDEPENDENT arm-1 monolithic glycolysis instances (bulk-bound TelluriumProcess), each advanced on a DIFFERENT geometrically-spaced interval (fastest -> slowest, the slow tail overrunning the run horizon). The instances share no store and are uncoupled, so there is no operator-splitting error — each is just the arm-1 monolith on its own clock. The composite is run under scheduler="scan" (stock O(P^2) tick loop) and scheduler="heap" (#270's event-min-heap, O(P log P)); the Task-4 timing harness times run() alone (construction excluded) for P in {4,16,64,128,256}.
claim: process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler is bit-identical to the stock scan loop (same math, different tick order) and its wall-clock advantage grows monotonically with P on a genuinely multi-rate composite — measured 0.98x at P=4 (heap bookkeeping with nothing to gain), crossing over near P~50-64, to 1.64x at P=256 on real libroadrunner/CVODE instances. The per-process CVODE integration dominates the per-tick scan until P reaches the low hundreds, so the multiplier is modest at the P a unit test can afford; it is reported as measured, and the regime where it grows large (hundreds-to-thousands of cheap processes) is #270's own 4.8x@P=100 -> 46x@P=1000 micro-benchmark, cited not reproduced.

expected_behavior.name: arm7-heap-beats-scan-at-scale
expected_behavior.observable: scan (stock O(P^2)) vs heap (#270 O(P log P)) run wall-clock, and their speedup, vs the instance count P
expected_behavior.condition: scan and heap produce bit-identical final state at every P (same math, different scheduler); the heap/scan speedup rises monotonically with P and exceeds 1 at the largest measured P (heap faster)
expected_behavior.rationale: a many-rate composite is exactly the O(P^2) case the event-heap scheduler was built to fix; because only the tick ordering changes, correctness must be identical and only wall-clock may differ.

findings.summary: Scan and heap are bit-identical at every measured P — multirate_scaling records a per-N bit_identical flag (np.array_equal of the two schedulers' final state across every instance store), True at each of P=4..256, and a dedicated test asserts it across the measured Ns (not just the small-N case). #270 changes only the order in which due processes are popped, never the math. The multi-rate composite is uncoupled (independent monoliths, empty inputs), so there is no operator-splitting divergence to confound the timing.

Measured scan vs heap run() wall-clock (median of 3, construction excluded), geometric intervals i_fast=H/(3P)..i_slow=3H, H=20: P=4 scan=0.0082s heap=0.0083s (0.98x); P=16 0.0468s / 0.0492s (0.95x); P=64 0.419s / 0.371s (1.13x); P=128 1.555s / 1.280s (1.22x); P=256 6.598s / 4.019s (1.64x). The heap/scan speedup rises monotonically with P and crosses over near P~50-64.

Honesty: heap is ~5% SLOWER at tiny P (P=4,16) — the event-heap bookkeeping has nothing to gain when the per-tick scan is trivially short — exactly #270's documented single-rate penalty. The win is modest (<=1.64x) at the P a test can afford because the real libroadrunner/CVODE update per due process dominates the per-tick Python scan at small P (measured crossover ~P=50-64). #270's cheap-process micro-benchmark (where the scheduler is the whole cost) is 4.8x@P=100 rising to 46x@P=1000; arm 7 reproduces the TREND with real integrator instances, not those multipliers.

Scheduler API used (#270): the strategy is the "scheduler" CONFIG FIELD on the Composite (Composite({"state": doc, "scheduler": "heap"|"scan"|"auto"}, core=core)); "auto" (the default) picks heap only when more than one distinct process interval is present. Arm 7 selects "scan" vs "heap" explicitly to measure both.
